Node's Process Model vs. PHP's

Why a plain array in ticket.service.js can act as shared storage across every request.

Look again at Figure 1.8 (previous slide): tickets and nextId are declared with let, at the top of the file, outside any function. Every request that calls createTicket pushes onto that same array, and the next request's call to getAllTickets sees it. There's no database yet — so how is that state surviving between separate HTTP requests?

This is the Node process model from the very first topic of this lesson, now showing up in real code. Recall: a PHP-FPM worker restarts fresh for every request, so a plain PHP variable never survives past the request that created it — you'd have needed a database, a file, or a session even to fake this. A Node process, by contrast, starts once (when you run npm run dev) and keeps running, handling every request that arrives on the same live process, with the same JavaScript memory intact the whole time.

PHP-FPM:  [request 1: fresh process] → [request 2: fresh process] → ...
                 ↑ variables die here      ↑ variables die here

Node:     [ one process, started once ] → handles request 1, 2, 3, ... in turn
                 ↑ module-level variables (tickets, nextId) live here the whole time

That's what lets let tickets = [...] at the top of ticket.service.js act as a (very temporary) shared data store across requests, with zero extra plumbing. It's also exactly why this is only a Week 1 stand-in: that same array is shared by every request Express is currently handling, with no isolation and no persistence across restarts — restart the process (or deploy a second instance, eventually) and it resets to the two seeded tickets. Week 2 replaces it with a real database specifically so ticket data survives a restart and isn't just sitting in one process's memory.
